bio.en: Sanchan Saxena is VP of Product at Coinbase and was previously Head of Product and GM at Airbnb, founder and Head of Product of Instagram Shopping, Director of Product at Yahoo, and a PM at Microsoft.
bio.zh: Sanchan Saxena 是 Coinbase 的产品副总裁，此前曾任 Airbnb 产品负责人兼总经理、Instagram Shopping 创始人兼产品负责人、Yahoo 产品总监，以及微软产品经理。

summary.en: Sanchan shares the inside story of how Airbnb navigated COVID when travel stopped, and the lessons he learned from working alongside exceptional CEOs like Brian Chesky, Brian Armstrong, and Kevin Systrom. He covers how to set up a product development process at a startup, when to hire your first PM, and when (and when not) to A/B test. The episode is full of hard-won wisdom from scaling products at the world's top companies.
summary.zh: Sanchan 分享了 Airbnb 在疫情导致旅行停摆时如何渡过难关的内幕，以及他与 Brian Chesky、Brian Armstrong、Kevin Systrom 等杰出 CEO 共事所学到的经验。他涵盖了如何在初创公司建立产品开发流程、何时招聘第一位 PM，以及何时（以及何时不）该做 A/B 测试。本期充满了在世界顶级公司规模化产品过程中锤炼出的硬核智慧。

turns.speaker: Sanchan Saxena
turns.en: Thank you, Lenny, for inviting me. Excited to be here and chat with you today.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，莱尼，邀请我来这里。很高兴能和大家交流。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely. My pleasure. I was really lucky to work with you at Airbnb for many years, where you were a beloved product leader. And then you went on to do bigger and better things now at Coinbase. And I'd love to just hear how you first got into product, and then just a little bit of your journey of how you got to where you're today, where you're basically head of product at Coinbase.
turns.zh: 当然，荣幸之至。能在Airbnb与你共事多年，我深感幸运——你曾是备受尊敬的产品负责人。而如今你在Coinbase开创了更宏大的事业。我很想听听你最初是如何踏入产品领域的，以及你如何一步步走到今天的位置——如今你已是Coinbase的产品负责人。

turns.speaker: Sanchan Saxena
turns.en: Yeah, happy to answer. Maybe I'll go back in time and start from my first job. I was in my third year of engineering where the entrepreneurial bug caught me, so to say, bit me. And I took a little bit of sabbatical from my engineering, which by the way, was in aerospace engineering. (00:04:03): I wanted to be an astronaut, go to space. Unfortunately back then, there wasn't an Elon Musk for SpaceX. If you wanted to go to space, you got to work for a government agency, which I didn't like. Fast forward that to my third year of engineering and I start my company, raised a bunch of money, hired some people. (00:04:18): Didn't go as planned, so I [inaudible 00:04:20], came back and finished my engineering and got a job at Microsoft, which made my mom very happy. My mom said, "My son finally has a stable job. What the heck he was doing running some companies?" But jokes aside, I got a job at Microsoft, which was a great starting position. (00:04:34): I started in engineering. But within a year or so, I moved into product. And I moved to the Silicon Valley office of Microsoft. Never worked in Seattle, but always worked in Silicon Valley at Mountain View. And I worked for this product called Hotmail. I don't know how many people know this or not, but there's an email service called Hotmail. I was one of the product people.
turns.zh: 好的，我很乐意分享。或许我该从头说起。大三那年，我被创业的热情点燃，暂停了航天工程学的学业。（00:04:03）当时我梦想成为宇航员，探索太空。但遗憾的是，那个年代还没有马斯克领导的SpaceX。想进入太空领域就得加入政府机构，而这并非我所向往。转眼间，我创办了自己的公司，筹集了大量资金，招募了团队。（00:04:18）结果事与愿违，我选择退学，回到微软工作。（00:04:20）我妈妈听说后很不满：“你儿子终于找到稳定工作了，之前折腾那些公司干什么？”不过玩笑归玩笑，微软确实是个绝佳的起点。（00:04:34）我从工程师做起，但一年左右就转入产品部门，搬到了微软的硅谷总部。从未在西雅图工作过，一直在山景城的硅谷办公室待着。我参与的产品叫Hotmail。不知道大家是否还记得，这个邮箱服务曾风靡一时，我就是其中的产品负责人之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Absolutely. It's scary that people may not even know what Hotmail is at this point.
turns.zh: 确实令人惊讶，如今可能很多人都不知道Hotmail是什么了。

turns.speaker: Sanchan Saxena
turns.en: Right? It's kind of crazy. Back in the day, it was pretty cool. I worked there, and then since then have been in Silicon Valley. So moved into product back in, I think, 2005 or '06, something like that, and since then been in product. I've been very lucky and fortunate to have stumbled upon incredible opportunities all the way from Facebook and Instagram to Airbnb and Coinbase. (00:05:16): And fun fact, when I joined Instagram, it was still very small. And it was less than, I think, 50 engineers or something like that. Very tiny. It was pre-revenue. We made $0 in revenue. I still remember the day when Zuck told Kevin Systrom we got to go make revenue, and we made $0 back then. (00:05:30): And was there till 2017. By the time it was like a billion monthly active users, multiple billion dollars in revenue, was my first hypergrowth experience as a product leader. And then in 2017, I joined Airbnb, which is where you and I worked together. There I had a dual role. (00:05:45): I was a GM of Airbnb Plus, but also the head of product helping Brian Chesky scale the product management organization, establish the culture of it, and see how best we can build a world class part organization. And then after that, I took some time off, about six months, introspective to see what do I want to do next. (00:06:00): And that is when I went into the Web 3.0 rabbit home, and that's when I learned more and more about Web 3.0, what's happening over there. I've always been investor in crypto since 2014, but never thought of it as a builder. I was like, "Ah, I don't know if I want to build in there. It seems cool. I can participate from the outside." (00:06:18): But then the more I read, the more I realized, "Man, this is one of the biggest revolutions happening." And that's when I joined Coinbase and here I'm the VP product for ecosystems and a bunch of other stuff that I do here, and excited to be able to play a small role in this next revolution called Web 3.0.
turns.zh: 是吧？这真是太不可思议了。回想起来，那段时光确实很酷。我曾在那里工作过，之后便去了硅谷。大概2005年或2006年，我转入产品部门，从那以后就一直从事产品工作。能从Facebook、Instagram到Airbnb和Coinbase，一路遇到这么多绝佳的机会，我深感幸运。（00:05:16）：说个趣事，我加入Instagram时，它还很小。当时工程师不到50人左右，规模很小，还没开始盈利。我至今还记得扎克伯格对凯文·西斯特罗姆说‘我们得去赚钱’，而当时我们一分钱收入都没有。（00:05:30）：我在那里一直待到2017年。到那时，Instagram每月活跃用户已破十亿，营收数十亿美元。这是我作为产品负责人的首次高增长体验。2017年，我加入Airbnb，就是你和我共事过的那家公司。在那里，我身兼两职：既是Airbnb Plus的总经理，又是产品负责人——帮助布莱恩·切斯基扩建产品管理团队，建立团队文化，并探索如何打造世界级的产品组织。之后，我休息了大约六个月，进行自我反思，思考下一步该做什么。（00:06:00）：就在那时，我深入Web 3.0领域，了解了Web 3.0的现状和未来趋势。自2014年起我就一直是加密货币投资者，但从未想过自己会成为从业者。当时我觉得，‘哦，我不知道自己是否想参与其中。虽然它很酷，但我更倾向于作为旁观者参与。’（00:06:18）：但随着深入研究，我意识到，‘天哪，这可是正在发生的最大革命之一。’于是我加入了Coinbase，现在担任生态系统产品副总裁，负责一系列相关工作，很高兴能在Web 3.0这场新革命中发挥微小作用。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. Just listening into that trajectory and places that you worked, I imagine people are wondering like, "Man, how do I follow a trajectory like that? How do I live a life like Sanchan?" Do you have any advice for someone that's maybe just starting out that may be wondering like, "How do I follow this sort of path? How do I work at all these incredible companies and get to maybe where you are now?"?
turns.zh: 太不可思议了。听完你的职业发展历程和工作经历，我想人们肯定会好奇：“天哪，我该如何追随这样的轨迹？如何过上像Sanchan这样的生活？”对于刚起步的人，你有什么建议吗？比如，“如何走上这样的职业道路？如何在这些优秀的公司工作，最终达到你现在的成就？”

turns.speaker: Sanchan Saxena
turns.en: Yeah, I look back at my career, one thing that is very true is that I never had that plan. I stumbled upon a lot of things. I mean, I wanted to be an aerospace engineer, didn't work out, pivoted. I started my own company, didn't work out, pivoted. I came to Silicon Valley, worked at Hotmail, didn't work out, pivoted. (00:07:07): Things start to materialize when you actually take steps to do something. My biggest advice to people is, oftentimes the analysis paralysis of dotting every eye, crossing every tee sometimes chokes you out of opportunities. When you find something that gives you energy, just jump in with both feet. And try to go through that process, and pivot and learn, and pivot and learn and pivot. (00:07:29): That's how you would create a great career as opposed to sort of a five year career plan and working backwards from that. Those things just don't work. The other thing I would say is I read this book early on in my life called the Little Bets. It actually was a reflection of whatever I did in my life. Before that I thought I was a weirdo, I don't know what I'm doing. And then I read that book and I realized, "Oh my God, there's some method to my madness. It's called little bets." (00:07:52): You take little bets, you try them out. If they don't work out, you build rapid recovery and start to do something else. And that is the meta story connecting all the dots in my life, in all the career opportunities that I've had, just one piece of big advice I'll tell everybody. The second thing I'll say is product management is a very interesting discipline. (00:08:10): You don't go to school for that. You don't get a degree for that. And most people that I know in product have stumbled upon product management. They were doing something else and like, "Oh my God, this seems cool. I want to do this." The advice I give early stage product people is you got to learn the art and the science of product management early on in your career. (00:08:29): There's an art piece to it and then there's a science piece to it, and you got to be able to manage both of those things in your head. If you become too scientific, you miss out on opportunities because you can't see those opportunities using the scientific method of discovery, because they're too tiny or they're so farfetched that people cannot even understand them. (00:08:45): And the art piece is really important for you to be able to sniff those out by being in the community, hanging out with people who are actually builders and learning where the next trends would be. My advice to people is go get a job which will make you the fastest learner in the field of product management. (00:09:00): That is what will help you a lot. No course, no degree, none of those things will help. The most important thing will be how quickly can you jump in, learn the auto product management. Some people prefer doing that at a startup. Some people prefer doing it at a established fan company, which has processes and systems as well. It's your choice. But the fastest you learn that, the better it'll get for you.
turns.zh: 是啊，当我回顾自己的职业生涯时，有一点非常明显——我从未制定过详细的规划。很多事情都是机缘巧合。比如，我原本想成为一名航空航天工程师，但没能如愿，转而另辟蹊径。我创办了自己的公司，却以失败告终。来到硅谷后，我在Hotmail工作，也未能成功。（00:07:07）当你真正采取行动时，事情往往会水到渠成。我给别人的最大建议是：面对分析瘫痪症时，别再纠结于细节，否则你会错失良机。当你找到能激发热情的事物时，就全身心投入其中，不断试错、调整、学习，再调整、再学习、再调整。这才是构建卓越职业生涯的秘诀，而非遵循五年规划倒推的死板模式。那些方法根本行不通。另外，我年轻时读过一本书叫《小赌博》，它让我意识到自己多年来所做的一切都遵循着这个理念。此前我总觉得自己是个怪人，迷茫无措。读完这本书后，我恍然大悟：“天啊，我的疯狂行为其实是有方法论的，那叫‘小赌博’。” （00:07:52）你可以先小规模尝试，如果失败，迅速调整方向，再接再厉。这就是我人生各个阶段、每个职业机遇的连接线，也是我给所有人的重要建议。第二点是，产品管理是一门非常有趣的学科。（00:08:10）没人教你这门技能，也没有相关学位。我认识的大多数产品经理都是误打误撞进入这个领域的。他们原本在做其他工作，突然发现：“哇，这太酷了，我想尝试。” 我给初级产品经理的建议是：尽早掌握产品管理的艺术与科学。（00:08:29）这门学科既有艺术性，也有科学性，你必须能在脑海中兼顾两者。如果过于理性，就会错失机会，因为科学方法无法识别微小的、看似天马行空的机遇。（00:08:45）而艺术性部分至关重要，你需要通过融入社区、与真正的产品创造者交流，提前捕捉下一个趋势。我的建议是：找一份能让你快速成长的产品管理工作。这才是关键。课程、学位统统无用，唯有快速上手至关重要。有些人选择初创公司，有些人青睐成熟大厂，但选择权在你手中。越快掌握核心技能，你就能越早收获回报。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I love so much about that advice. To go a little bit further on this last point. When people are looking for a company to go join to learn, to accelerate their career the way you're describing, what do you think they should be looking for? I know you said maybe a startup. Do you think they should join a startup? Do you think they should join a bigger company? What kind of things should you look for to find the best place to learn?
turns.zh: 哇。我特别喜欢你提到的这些建议。再深入探讨一下最后一点。当人们寻找一家能让他们快速提升职业生涯的公司时，你认为他们应该关注哪些方面？我知道你提到或许可以考虑初创公司，但你觉得他们应该加入初创公司吗？还是更适合大公司？要找到最适合学习的环境，应该关注哪些方面？

turns.speaker: Sanchan Saxena
turns.en: Yeah, I think there is no right recipe for one, but it matters to the individual. I'll share both stories with you. The way to think about this is let's say you want to get to a destination, whichever destination it is, you probably want to get on the faster ship. You don't want to get on a slower ship. That's one metaphor to use in your mind. (00:09:58): And then when you got to the ship, you know the ship will get there, but remember you are not going to get to your destination faster than the ship will. You got to understand what your destination is, then optimize the learnings from there. At a startup, you're going to learn a lot of things. There are three types of learning, a starter learning, meaning you can get started. You're a person who can get started. You see an idea, you see an opportunity, you can get started. Right? (00:10:21): That is something that a startup will teach you a lot. You see something, you want to get started to do something about it, great, you'll learn a lot over it. And there's zero to one people who can then take what they have started and scale it to one. And then there are one and beyond people who are scalers, who will scale the system that is found product market fit. (00:10:38): And I think depending on your journey, depending on your career, depending upon where you are, you might want to optimize for different types of learnings as well. What I advise people is there's a great way to go to Google, Facebook and Amazon and learn the scale mechanisms that these companies have built. And I look at Amazon and I get inspired by that company, because what they have figured out is how to scale innovation with 1 million employees. (00:10:59): It's a pretty different learning. And you can't potentially find that at a startup. Similarly, the ability to just get started, the ability to see an idea, start hacking at it, start building it without the encumbrances of the processes and the system that these big organizations have, you can probably learn that in a big company as well. You got to figure out what are you optimizing for, what goes well with you. (00:11:23): I've seen many successful leaders who will get choked up in a big company environment, and I've seen many big company successful executives who want to choke up in a very startup environment. And this is not for everybody. Both sides of the games are not for everybody. First and foremost recognizing what gives you energy, recognizing where you thrive the most is really important. (00:11:41): For example, I am not the guy who can optimize a 100,000 employee company. I will never enjoy that kind of learning. I've done to some extent a large company thing, but I thrive in that starter to scale angle. But when it becomes too large, I start to lose interest in that kind of learning. Some people enjoy different things. You got to understand what it is and be able to optimize there.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为没有放之四海而皆准的标准方案，但这取决于个人情况。我可以跟你分享两个案例。思考这个问题时，不妨设想你想抵达某个目的地，无论这个目的地是什么，你可能都希望搭乘速度更快的船只。而不是更慢的船。这是可以用作思维比喻的一个概念。（00:09:58）当你登上这艘船时，你知道船会带你抵达目的地，但要记住，你的学习速度永远赶不上船的速度。你必须先明确自己的目标，然后从中优化学习效果。在初创公司，你能学到很多东西。学习分为三种类型：启动型学习，即你能迅速上手；你是一个能快速行动的人。一旦看到一个想法或机会，就能立刻行动起来。这正是初创公司能教会你的东西。看到机会后，你想行动，那很棒，你会从中收获很多。而零到一型人才能够将已启动的事业扩展至规模化阶段。一型及以上型人才是扩张型人才，他们能将找到的产品市场匹配的系统进行规模化。（00:10:38）我认为，根据个人经历、职业发展阶段和所处环境的不同，你可能需要优化不同类型的学习效果。我建议人们去谷歌、Facebook和亚马逊学习这些公司建立的规模化机制。我观察亚马逊时，深受其启发，因为他们成功破解了如何在100万员工规模下实现创新规模化的难题。这是一种截然不同的学习体验，而这在初创公司中很难获得。同样，在大公司中，你也能学习到快速上手、识别机会并无阻碍地开始构建的能力——即便没有大公司那些繁琐的流程和系统。你必须明确自己的优化目标，找到最适合自己的方向。（00:11:23）我见过许多在大公司环境中感到窒息的成功领导者，也见过许多想在初创环境中同样感到不适的大公司高管。这种选择并非适合所有人。大公司和初创公司的游戏规则都不是为所有人量身打造的。首先，要认识到什么能给你能量，什么是你的最佳成长环境，这至关重要。（00:11:41）比如，我无法优化一个拥有10万员工的公司。我永远无法享受那种学习体验。我在某种程度上体验过大公司的生活，但我更擅长从启动到规模化的过程。一旦规模过大，我对那种学习的兴趣就会逐渐消失。不同的人有不同的偏好，你必须理解自己的特质，并据此优化环境。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Where would you say you learned the most of all the companies you worked at that helped accelerate your career most?
turns.zh: 您认为在您曾就职过的所有公司中，哪家对您的职业生涯助力最大？

turns.speaker: Sanchan Saxena
turns.en: I think I would rank Airbnb probably the place that I learned the most. And I'll share with you and your audience why I feel that way. I joined Airbnb back in 2017, making decent revenue, had good product market fit. I remember when I got there, the entire product management order was like 30 people or 40 people, something like that. (00:12:26): You had three directors of product, very small still for a company that was generating a billion plus dollars in revenue. And then the context was there was this ambitious founder, Brian, who will never take no for an answer. And he would bend reality in many regards to make shit happen. (00:12:41): And you are very familiar with those days as well, but you will have a practicability. You will leave the review thinking, "Shit, this is actually possible." The guy just inspired you that this is actually possible and you went in thinking it's not possible. (00:12:52): What I found is that at Airbnb, I learned a bunch of different things. One, I learned how to build products where software is just one part of the product. Let me explain that a little bit. The product of Airbnb isn't the app. It is a means to an end. The product of Airbnb is the memories you're going to create when you sit in that Airbnb beautiful house with your family, with your friends, and you're building those memories. That's the product. It's in real world. (00:13:18): And how you build a real world product which is of course powered by software, like the app, the website, et cetera, is different than just building a pure product that is purely software. I learned what is operations, how to scale operations, how to work with operations, how to create beautiful physical homes over there. The second thing I learned is just how to build great products. (00:13:39): I mean, I got I think a masterclass from Chesky in how to build products by watching him act, behave, and make decisions as well. And we'll talk about it later today. But I learned some of my fundamental product principles from him, and working with him and the team that he had assembled, the design leaders, the engineering leaders, et cetera. I learned a lot over there. (00:13:59): And last one but not least, there was still a hypergrowth thing. We were going through crazy growth. And then I learned what happens in leadership when coronavirus happens, the company starts to tank. It was a lesson in crisis management. I tell my friends I could not have gone to HBS Stanford business school to learn crisis management as much as I learned while being in the front row seat managing through that. (00:14:23): My learning as a product leader from Brian as a hyperscaler, taking the product management organization from 30, 40 people to 200 people, and last but not the least, managing the crisis. I felt like it all compressed into three years something that you will learn in 30.
turns.zh: 我觉得Airbnb可能是让我学到最多的地方。接下来，我想和您以及听众分享我为何这么认为。我在2017年加入Airbnb，当时公司营收不错，产品与市场契合度也很高。我记得刚到那里时，整个产品管理团队只有30到40人，规模不算大。但当时公司创始人布莱恩野心勃勃，永不言败，他会不择手段把事情搞定。（00:12:26）您对那段时光应该也很熟悉，但当时更侧重于实用性——听完分享会后，您会感叹“天啊，这居然可行！”他总能激发你的潜能，让你从认为不可能到最终实现。（00:12:52）在Airbnb，我学到了很多东西。首先，我学会了如何打造软件只是产品一部分的完整产品。举个例子，Airbnb的产品不是应用程序，而是达成目标的手段。当您与家人、朋友在Airbnb的漂亮房子里创造美好回忆时，这才是真正的产品。（00:13:18）如何打造现实世界的产品（当然也离不开软件支持，比如应用程序、网站等），与纯粹的软件产品有本质区别。我还掌握了运营知识，学会了如何扩展运营规模，与运营团队合作，打造实体美宅。第二点是如何打造伟大的产品。（00:13:39）我从切斯基身上学到了产品设计的精髓，通过观察他的行为和决策来领悟。今天我们会详细探讨，但我从他和他组建的团队——设计负责人、工程负责人等——那里学到了许多基础产品原则。在那里我收获颇丰。（00:13:59）最后但同样重要的是，公司经历了高速增长。我们疯狂扩张。但新冠疫情来袭时，领导层如何应对危机管理，这也是一堂深刻的危机管理课。我跟朋友说，即便去哈佛商学院学习危机管理，也比不上亲身经历的这堂课。（00:14:23）作为产品负责人，从布莱恩的超大规模管理中学习——将30、40人的产品管理团队扩展至200人，以及危机管理经验——这些都浓缩在三年的时光里，而这份收获本应需要30年的积累。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine you had no sense of that sort of path or trajectory or learning when you joined Airbnb, it was like, "Hmm, this is going to be a great company, little [inaudible 00:14:46] things."
turns.zh: 我猜您加入Airbnb时并未预见到这样的发展路径或学习曲线，只是觉得“嗯，这会是一家很棒的公司，有一些小细节需要注意”。

turns.speaker: Sanchan Saxena
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. And oftentimes it's a joke, but I'll say it out anyhow. Oftentimes you meet leaders who are leaving Facebook, Amazon, Google, and it's like, "Hey, here's my Excel spreadsheet. Here's how I imagine the startup that I'm joining will grow. Here's the valuation. Here's my life. Here's my compensation. That's it." None of that shit is going to happen. (00:15:05): The companies have a different trajectory and you can't predict those things. So yeah, you're right. When I joined Airbnb, I thought it's going to be a walk in the park, just like Instagram was. I mean, Instagram wasn't a walk in the park. But relatively speaking, Instagram never experienced this kind of rapid pivoting of the reality, right? (00:15:22): I'll share with you I was there when Instagram had less than a hundred million monthly active users, $0 in revenue, 50 engineers, till it had 1 billion monthly active users, billions of dollars in revenue and thousands of employees. And I don't remember a time where the reality got bended so badly that we had to pivot. (00:15:41): In Airbnb's time, man, one fine morning in January, Brian and us were all talking about going IPO and taking the company public. Six weeks later, we are figuring out, "Damn, how do we make this company survive?" The revenues, if I'm not wrong, dropped to less in single digits of last year's revenue. (00:16:00): And there is no head of product, there is no CFO, there is no COO, whoever has a business plan to say, "Hmm, what are we going to do when our revenue drops to single digits of last year's revenue?" (00:16:10): I definitely didn't think that is what happened, but that's what ended up happening. Luckily, everything worked out, and I'm happy to share what we did and how we navigated through that with the audience, but it was some crazy, crazy times, man.
turns.zh: 是啊，那是肯定的。很多时候这不过是个玩笑，但我还是要说出来。经常会遇到从Facebook、亚马逊、谷歌离职的领导，他们会说：“嘿，这是我的Excel表格。这是我对即将加入的初创公司的增长预期。这是估值。这是我的生活。这是我的薪酬。就这样。”但这些事根本不会发生。（00:15:05）：这些公司的发展轨迹各不相同，你根本无法预测这些变化。所以你说得对。我加入Airbnb时，以为会像加入Instagram一样轻松。说实话，Instagram也并不容易。但相对而言，Instagram从未经历过现实与预期如此巨大的偏差，对吧？（00:15:22）：我可以告诉你，当Instagram月活用户还不到一亿、收入为零、只有50名工程师时，到用户数达到10亿、营收数十亿美元、员工数千人时，我不记得有哪次现实与预期严重偏差到必须调整策略。（00:15:41）：在Airbnb时期，1月某个晴朗的早晨，布莱恩和我们还都在讨论上市计划。六周后，我们却在想：“该死，如何让公司渡过难关？”如果我没记错的话，营收已经跌至去年同期的个位数。（00:16:00）：没有产品负责人、没有CFO、没有COO，没有人拿出商业计划说：“嗯，营收跌至去年同期的个位数，我们该怎么办？” （00:16:10）：我绝对没想到会这样，但最终就是这样了。幸运的是，一切都解决了。我很乐意和听众分享我们的应对之策，但那真是疯狂至极的时期。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I was on the outside of that having left Airbnb a couple years prior and I was like, "Shit, what am I going to do now? I've been taking time off. There go all my Airbnb shares. I think I can get a job soon." And that's actually what led to the newsletter and starting to charge for the newsletter. But I'm very thankful for the turnaround that you helped create. I'd actually love to hear a bit more about what it is they did that helped them through that.
turns.zh: 我当时不在其中——我几年前就离开了Airbnb。我当时想：“妈的，现在该怎么办？我一直在休假。我的Airbnb股票也没了。我应该能很快找到新工作。”这实际上促使我创办了这份时事通讯，并开始收费。但我非常感激你们帮助公司渡过难关的转变。我很想听听你们具体做了哪些事来渡过难关。

turns.speaker: Sanchan Saxena
turns.en: I'll share with you the behind the scenes story that we went through. This is January, and Brian had this idea of taking the company public in April. And we are working on the road show deck, we are working through numbers, we were crafting the story, et cetera, everything's going well. (00:16:59): And then we hear of this coronavirus crisis and all of a sudden countries are shutting down, one after the other. Italy shuts down. Japan shuts down. This country shuts down. And all of a sudden we can see on our travel map, we have this dashboard where you can see where people are traveling, and you can see travel goes down to zero in this country on a map. This goes down to zero in this country, and you're like, "Holy shit, what's happening over here?" (00:17:19): I remember in all-hands where Brian stood up and said, "Look, we built this company for a crisis like this. We built this company, we have $2 billion in bank." I think something like that, some ridiculous number. "We have not used a single amount of money from our last raise," because we were profitable or growing really profitable. "And we are going to survive this." (00:17:35): Six weeks later, he's in the same all-hands and telling people, "This is a different world we are living in." We had to lay off 1,900 employees, just 190 of those were in my organization. We had to raise $2 billion in debt, and the valuation dropped to 50% of what the valuation was. It was one of the craziest times. (00:17:53): And Lenny, when you go through that, the loss of challenges you face, one is fine. You can cut costs by laying off employees for a little bit and create a little bit more runway. But remember, this is coronavirus time. I had to let go of people over Zoom. I couldn't even meet them in-person. (00:18:09): I still remember when I actually finished my speech and I told them, "This is the last day," now, I literally shed a tear in front of everybody, because I was like, "Man, this is hard. This is really, really hard." And the company let go of 1900 people. I just had to let go of 190 in my organization, but it was still very painful, because remember, it is no fault of these employees. They just happen to be at the wrong side of the tornado that's hitting the world. (00:18:34): The second equally most important thing was the people who stayed back, how do you motivate them? One is you can let go of the people, but people who stayed back, they need a light of hope that something is going to turn around. But how do you plan when data is changing every single day? And every day we will wake up, a new country will go down and say, "No, no more travels into our market". (00:18:56): And we start predicting that our revenue will be 7, 10, some ridiculous very small percent of last years. There's panic. And this is where I would say Brian Chesky is an incredible leader. He's the Rocky Balboa of Silicon valley. You can punch him, he'll go down, he'll stand up, he'll fight again. That's the analogy. He's truly the Rocky Balboa where he took so many punches, but he stood up again and say, "One more round." (00:19:22): And that's how the company survived. From an operating principle, we went into two week planning mode. Greg Greeley, who was the president of Airbnb used to say, "Look, can't plan for a year, can't plan for a quarter. We're going to plan every two weeks. We're going to react to every two weeks." And I think this is the lesson that I try to share with a lot of product people as well and founders as well is that things are going to go all right. Things are not going to go as you plan. (00:19:47): The real genius isn't to dot every eye, to cross every team before you get started. The real genius is, what do you do when shit goes wrong? And I believe rapid recovery is the key to success. What you do, how quickly you can recover from failure becomes really important. Our operating model changed. We went to two weeks shipping. All right, what are we doing for the next two weeks? What is the most urgent thing for the company? For the company. Not my team, not your team, not somebody else's team. (00:20:13): And we pivoted the entire machinery down over there. And then slowly and slowly after two or three months, we got to a place where we got semblance of what is happening. I want to tell you one story. Hotels and Airbnb are competitors, right? And when this thing happened, we had a debate, "How are we going to position Airbnb against hotels?" And actually we had to figure out what are the advantages of people staying in an Airbnb. (00:20:35): And luckily for us, being in an Airbnb where the air you breathe is only you and your family turned out to be a huge secret sauce to compete. When you're in a hotel, there's a lobby. You get to be with other people. But when you're are in an Airbnb, you're safe. We pivoted our marketing as well and messaging as well. The entire company came together to become one. (00:20:55): And through this, I would say Brian's leadership was just phenomenal, everything I learned about crisis management, leading with calmness. There's a very good saying in boxing. I love sports. There's a very good saying, which is, you can have all the plan. The moment you step inside the boxing and you get a punch on your face, all your plans go out the window. And you got to stay calm when you get a punch on your face. (00:21:15): And that is what I learned from Brian, how to stay calm, how to stay composed while at the same time, deep down you know you owe a lot to these employees, you know you owe a lot to these employees to have clarity, and for them to stick around with you and believe in you that the company can turn around. It was an amazing journey, but pretty painful.
turns.zh:
我要和大家分享我们经历的幕后故事。这是1月份，布莱恩提出了在4月份让公司上市的想法。当时我们正在制作路演材料，核算数据，构思故事，一切进展顺利。（00:16:59）但随后我们听说了新冠病毒危机，各个国家突然相继封锁。意大利封锁了，日本封锁了，某个国家封锁了。突然在我们的旅行地图上，我们那个可以查看人们旅行情况的仪表盘显示，某个国家的旅行数据直线下降至零。另一个国家的数据也降至零，你会惊呼：“天啊，这里到底发生了什么？！”（00:17:19）我记得在全员大会上，布莱恩站起来说：“看，我们为应对这样的危机而创立了这家公司。我们手握20亿美元的银行存款。”好像是这么个天文数字。“我们上一轮融资的资金一分钱都没用过”，因为当时公司盈利或增长态势良好。“我们一定能挺过这一关。”（00:17:35）六周后，他在同一场全员大会上告诉大家：“我们身处一个全新的世界。”我们裁减了1900名员工，其中190人在我的部门。不得不通过债务融资筹集20亿美元，公司估值暴跌至原来的50%。这是最疯狂的时期之一。（00:17:53）伦尼，当你经历这些挑战时，有些还可以应对。比如暂时裁员降低成本，争取更多缓冲时间。但要记住，这是在新冠疫情期间。我不得不在Zoom上通知裁员，甚至无法当面告知员工。（00:18:09）我至今记得结束演讲时对他们说：“今天是最后一天。”当着所有人的面流下眼泪，因为我心想：“天啊，这太难了。真的太难了。” 公司裁掉了1900人，我部门只裁了190人，但依然心痛不已，毕竟这些员工没有任何过错，他们只是不幸处在席卷全球的风暴漩涡的错误一侧。（00:18:34）同样重要的是留下来的人——如何激励他们？一方面可以裁员，但留下的人需要看到希望的曙光，相信情况会好转。但数据每天都在变化，我们每天醒来都会发现又有国家关闭边境，宣布“不准入境”。（00:18:56）我们开始预测收入将是去年同期的7%、10%，甚至更低的微不足道的百分比。恐慌情绪蔓延。在我看来，布莱恩·切斯基是一位了不起的领导者。他是硅谷的洛奇·巴尔博亚。你可以重重打击他，他会倒下，但又会站起来继续战斗。这就是类比。他就像洛奇·巴尔博亚，尽管承受了无数打击，却一次次挺身而出，高呼“再打一轮！”（00:19:22）这就是公司如何渡过难关。从运营层面来说，我们进入了两周规划模式。Airbnb总裁格雷格·格里利曾说：“我们不能规划一年，也不能规划一个季度。我们要每两周规划一次，根据每两周的情况调整策略。” 我认为这是我试图与许多产品经理和创始人分享的经验：事情总会好起来的。只是不会按照你的预期发展。
计划。（00:19:47）：真正的天才之处不在于在开始前把所有细节都考虑到位，而在于当事情出错时该如何应对。我认为快速恢复是成功的关键。你的行动速度、从失败中恢复的速度变得至关重要。我们的运营模式发生了变化，我们改为两周发货周期。好吧，那接下来两周我们要做什么？对公司而言最紧迫的是什么？是公司，不是我的团队，不是你的团队，也不是其他人的团队。（00:20:13）我们把整个机器转移到了那边。然后，经过两三个月的逐步调整，我们才逐渐摸清了状况。我想讲一个故事。酒店和爱彼迎是竞争对手，对吧？当这场危机来临时，我们曾讨论过“如何让爱彼迎与酒店形成差异化竞争？”事实上，我们必须找出住在爱彼迎房源的优势所在。（00:20:35）幸运的是，住在爱彼迎房源里，呼吸的都是属于你和家人的空气，这竟成了一个绝佳的竞争秘诀。住在酒店时，会有大堂，得和其他客人共处。但在爱彼迎房源里，你能享有安全感。我们还调整了营销策略和宣传语，整个公司上下齐心协力。（00:20:55）通过这次经历，我要说布莱恩的领导力堪称卓越，我从他身上学到了危机管理的精髓——保持冷静应对。拳击界有句话说得好，我热爱体育运动，有句话是这样说的：你可以制定再多的计划，但当踏入拳台被对方一拳击中时，所有计划都会化为泡影。而当被击中时，必须保持冷静。（00:21:15）这就是我从布莱恩身上学到的，如何在保持冷静的同时，深知自己亏欠员工太多——他们需要清晰的思路，需要相信公司能东山再起。这是一段惊心动魄的旅程，但确实充满了阵痛。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wow. I haven't heard that level of detail about what went on inside, and so thank you for sharing all that. Very tactically, I'm curious, the two week planning cycles, how did that actually happen? Was there a large meeting every two weeks with the leaders and they just kind of discuss, "Here's where we're thinking for the next two weeks."?
turns.zh: 哇哦。我还从未听过如此详尽的内部运作细节，真是太感谢你分享这些了。从战术层面来讲，我很好奇，那个两周规划周期是如何具体运作的？是每两周召集一次高层会议，然后大家就坐在一起讨论：“接下来两周我们打算怎么做？”之类的吗？

turns.speaker: Sanchan Saxena
turns.en: Yeah, I think so. One of the things about Airbnb, and we'll talk about it later as well, but it's a very founder-driven company. While there are leaders over there, the founder is deeply in the trenches. He really understands the customer. He's not this executive who's so far removed from reality that they can't actually create the content. (00:22:04): Brian was living, breathing that exercise. Execs were breathing that thing. What we'll do is we'll have a bunch of things top-down. Again, this is what we need to do guys. We need to cut this feature. We need to cut this product line. We need to cut this business unit. I literally had to shut down one full business unit because we had to cut the bleeding, so to say, and let go of those many people. (00:22:24): It was a top-down mandate, but also it was a bottom-up. The engineers, the product managers and designers are frontline. They are in connection with the CX team who's hearing what customers are complaining about. And so there was a mixture of top-down guidance to a bottoms-up things that we are seeing on the field. And every two weeks or so, the leadership, Greg in that case, for example, would make a decision on, "Here are the things we are going to go handle." And there were no teams anymore. (00:22:50): We basically dissolved this idea that there are sub-teams. There was one team, #Airbnb. Didn't matter whether you worked in CX or Airbnb Plus or Lax, or any of those things, we're going to move engineers wherever we have to, we're going to move PMs wherever we need to, and there's no such thing as sub-team anymore. (00:23:09): A lot of engineers on my team would go on to do marketplace dynamic stuff, like pricing and all that stuff, while some of those engineers would then go on to build CX tools or something else that was needed for survival. I felt like a 4,000 people company was operating as a four people company and a 40 people company, which is one team, no sub-teams, everybody rowing in the same direction. And that was really important. (00:23:31): Because remember, employees who are at your company are looking for clarity. What should they work on? Is the thing that they're going to work on meaningful, right? Because nobody knows, right? And when people will ask you as a leader, like many people ask me, what does six months look like? What does a year look like? Where are we a year from now? (00:23:46): The most honest answer you can tell them is, "I don't know." Because if you cook shit up, they're going to see through that lie. They're going to like, "Ah, this is just all marketing fluff." We would be very honest as leaders, would be very vulnerable as leaders, saying, "This is truly once in a lifetime thing. We don't know how we're going to navigate. But here's what we believe to be true." (00:24:05): We had to get people from feature obsession, revenue obsession, to belief obsession. What is belief obsession? When we all believe that when coronavirus is over, people will want to travel. We all believe that coronavirus will be over. You start going into first principles belief-based thinking, and you'll bring stories that will make people believe that the future that we are working toward is actually possible. (00:24:28): For example, there was a survey we did, we said, "If money wasn't a consideration, what would you do for the rest of your life?" 99.99% of the people said, "I will travel the world." Travel is in human genes. And so we had to pivot to actually making people believe why travel will be back, why Airbnb will survive, and why Airbnb will eventually thrive if the coronavirus crisis is lower.
turns.zh:
是的，我觉得是这样的。Airbnb是一家由创始人主导的公司，虽然公司里有高层领导，但创始人始终亲自参与一线工作。他们真正理解客户需求，不像那些与现实脱节、无法创造真正价值的高管。（00:22:04）布莱恩全身心投入到那项工作中，而高管们也深受其影响。我们会从上至下推动变革，但最终还是要回归到一线。工程师、产品经理和设计师是前线力量，他们与客户体验团队保持紧密联系，及时了解用户反馈。这种自上而下的指导与一线实践相结合，每两周左右，领导层（比如格雷格）就会决定下一步行动：哪些功能要砍掉，哪些产品线要调整。不再有子团队概念，整个公司就是一个大团队。（00:22:50）我们打破了子团队的概念，所有团队都是#Airbnb的一部分。无论你是在客户体验部门、Airbnb Plus团队还是其他部门工作，我们都会根据需要调配工程师和产品经理，不再有子团队之分。（00:23:09）团队中的许多工程师会转去做市场动态相关的工作，如定价等，而另一些工程师则会开发客户体验工具或其他生存所需的功能。我感觉这家4000人的公司运作起来就像一个四人团队，40人的团队也像一个大团队，没有子团队，每个人都朝着同一个方向努力。这点至关重要。（00:23:31）记住，员工们希望清晰了解工作方向。他们的工作是否有意义？（因为没人能预知未来）当有人问你六个月后会怎样、一年后会怎样时，最诚实的回答就是“我不知道”。如果虚构数据，他们会识破虚伪。作为领导者，我们要保持真诚，坦然面对现实，说：“这是一生难得的机会，我们不知道如何前行，但我们坚信未来可期。”（00:24:05）我们要让员工从专注功能、专注收入转向专注信念。什么是信念？比如我们都相信新冠疫情结束后人们会重新旅行。我们从第一性原理出发，讲述故事，让人们相信我们描绘的未来是真实可行的。（00:24:28）比如我们做了一项调查：“如果不考虑金钱，你余生会做什么？” 99.99%的人回答“环游世界”。旅行是人类基因中固有的。因此，我们必须转变思维，让人们相信旅行会回归，Airbnb会存续，最终……
若新冠疫情危机得以缓解，经济将蓬勃发展。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: These stories are incredible. I was going to ask around the morale piece. You mentioned keeping morale up. And it sounds like a big piece of that was pulling people back to the mission and the vision of Airbnb and re-inspiring them, and helping them feel like this will work out. Is that what you found to be most effective, to keep more morale up, or is there anything else that also helped keep more morale up in this very tenuous time?
turns.zh: 这些故事太不可思议了。我本来想问问关于士气提升的部分。你提到要保持员工士气高涨。听起来在这种艰难时期，关键在于让员工重拾对Airbnb使命与愿景的信念，重新激发他们的斗志，让他们相信一切终将好转。在提升士气方面，你认为最有效的方法是什么？或者说，在这个至关重要的时期，还有哪些其他措施能有效维系士气？

turns.speaker: Sanchan Saxena
turns.en: I think in these tenuous times you will notice that you can't pay these employees better than market. When this happened, FAANG companies were at our door trying to poach our engineers. Overnight, every engineer was pinged by Facebook, Google say, "Hey, we heard Airbnb is going down. You want to come over? We'll pay you X amount of money, and that stock is stable." (00:25:34): You had vultures at the door, so to say, as a proverbial exercise where your top talent is getting poached, but you can't pay this top talent the best. Right? You can't. Because your financial situation doesn't allow you to do that, right? But you still give them something, right? Because it's at a lower price and you start to sell the vision that if the company turns around, this will be at a higher price and you'll have right compensation. But those were some of the challenges. (00:25:56): The second challenge is you'll notice that people who thrive in these situations will be the one who truly believe both in the mission, but I think more importantly in the founders to make that mission come to life. Because you and I both know, right, there are many companies who have the similar mission, want to do something similar, but some succeed and some don't. (00:26:17): And the secret sauce of that in my opinion is the founder. And if the employees do not believe in the founder, if the employees do not believe that the founder can make things happen as they talk about, and the founder is not able to connect with the employees, those companies go down in flames. The second thing I would say is the founder needs to be at the front line. And Brian Chesky was on the front line. (00:26:37): He was literally 24/7 available, interacting, making decisions, holding all-hands, writing emails, sending messages, and assuring people that I'm in this with you. By the way, there's a proverbial thing, right? When such situations happen, all execs take a pay cut. Every company does that, right? But then still certain companies survive, certain don't, right? (00:26:58): It's primarily because of the founder. And then the third thing I would say is somehow getting people to believe in the future that they came here to create. When drastic situations like these happens, when I joined Airbnb I had a vision of what it can become, and the reality snaps and all of a sudden like, "Holy shit. Is that even possible?" (00:27:21): That is the real art I learned from Brian is that the power of storytelling without any data. Your data is telling you, "You're going to die." The data is telling you, you got 7%, 10% of your revenue, whatever the number was now. I forget now. Like single digit number, right? (00:27:36): And every day you're seeing the numbers go down, right? And Brian has this incredible ability to help you see a future in a way so crystal clear that when you leave chatting with him, you're like, "Man, it's possible. We can make it happen. We can do it." That trait was really, really important that Brian invested in it, and all the three founders, by the way.
turns.zh: 我觉得在这种艰难时期，你会发现无法给员工开出高于市场的薪资。当这种情况发生时，FAANG公司（Facebook、亚马逊、苹果、谷歌、微软）纷纷来挖我们的工程师。突然间，每个工程师都收到Facebook、谷歌等公司的邮件：“嘿，我们听说Airbnb要倒闭了。你想来吗？我们会给你X金额的薪资，而且股票稳定。”（00:25:34）：可以说，这些巨头就是来挖人的，尤其是顶尖人才，但你又不能给他们开出最优薪资，对吧？因为财务状况不允许啊。但你还是要给他们一些希望，告诉他们如果公司能渡过难关，薪资就会提高，最终获得合理回报。但这些确实是挑战。（00:25:56）：第二个挑战是，你会发现那些在逆境中茁壮成长的人往往不仅深信Airbnb的使命，更重要的是，他们相信创始人能将使命变为现实。因为我们都知道，许多公司有相似的使命，想要做类似的事，但有些成功了，有些失败了。（00:26:17）：在我看来，秘诀在于创始人。如果员工不信任创始人，如果他们不相信创始人能兑现承诺，如果创始人无法与员工建立联系，那些公司注定失败。第二点是创始人必须亲自上阵。布莱恩·切斯基就亲力亲为。（00:26:37）：他每天24小时待命，参与决策、召开全员会议、回复邮件、发送消息，向员工保证“我会和你们共渡难关”。顺便说一句，有句话说得好，遇到这种情况，高管们都会降薪。每个公司都这么做，对吧？但有些公司能挺过去，有些则不行。（00:26:58）：这主要取决于创始人。第三点是如何让员工相信他们来这里是为了创造未来。当剧变发生时，比如我加入Airbnb时，我对它的愿景充满期待，但现实打破了幻想，突然间人们会说：“天啊，这真的可能吗？” （00:27:21）：我从布莱恩那里学到的最重要的技能，就是在没有数据支撑的情况下讲故事的能力。数据告诉你“你要倒闭了”，数据告诉你收入只剩7%、10%，具体数字我记不清了，反正是个位数。（00:27:36）：每天数据都在下滑，对吧？而布莱恩有种不可思议的能力，能让你清晰地看到未来，离开他办公室时你会感叹：“哇，原来真的有可能。我们能做到的。” 布莱恩和其他三位创始人对这项能力的投入实在太重要了。
